```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.2,
                      out.width = "100%")
```

A vector graphic stores the chart as shapes and text instead of pixels, so it stays sharp however
far it is zoomed in and however large it is printed. `plot_normal()` returns a ggplot object, so
`ggplot2::ggsave()` saves it in any of the vector formats below: the file extension names the
format, and `device` chooses how the file is written.

```{r setup}
library(snp)
```

The chart below is itself an SVG: zoom into the page and it stays sharp.

```{r demo, dev = "svg", fig.ext = "svg", fig.alt = "The standard normal curve, divided at every standard deviation and marked with the percentage of cases in each interval, above the z, T, cumulative percentage, percentile, sten, stanine, grade and IQ scales, drawn as an SVG."}
plot_normal()
```

## Which format

| Where the chart goes | Format | `device` |
|---|---|---|
| LaTeX, journals, printing | PDF | `cairo_pdf` |
| Web pages, Markdown, Word and PowerPoint | SVG | `svg` |
| Inkscape or Illustrator, to edit the text | SVG | `svglite::svglite` |
| Older versions of Word and PowerPoint | EMF | `devEMF::emf` |
| Journals that ask for EPS | EPS | `cairo_ps` |

## Size

`width` and `height` set the size of the figure, in inches unless `units` says otherwise. The chart
keeps its proportions, about 2.2 times as wide as it is tall with the standard scales, so a figure
with those proportions has no empty margins:

```{r size, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("normal.pdf", plot_normal(), width = 7, height = 3.2, device = cairo_pdf)
ggsave("normal.pdf", plot_normal(), width = 17.8, height = 8.2, units = "cm", device = cairo_pdf)
```

A vector graphic scales as a whole: shrink it in a document and its text shrinks with it. So save
it at the size it will be shown, and set `size`, the text size in millimetres, for that width. The
default of 3, about 8.5 points, suits a width of about 7 inches (17.8 cm); for other widths, scale
it in proportion, `size = 3 * width / 7` with the width in inches. A poster or a wide slide:

```{r wide, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("normal_wide.pdf", plot_normal(size = 5), width = 12, height = 5.6, device = cairo_pdf)
```

Below about 6 inches (15 cm) the text becomes small for print, so the chart reads best across the
full width of a page.

Every scale adds a row, and long scale names take width from the chart, so the right height
depends on both. For `n` scales it is about `width * (0.26 + 0.025 * n)` when the longest name is as
long as those of the standard scales, and about `width * (0.30 + 0.028 * n)` when every name is a
letter or two. Empty background at the sides means the figure is too short, and above and below,
too tall. Three scales with short names:

```{r height, eval = FALSE}
scales <- standard_normal_scales_data()
scales <- scales[scales$scale %in% c("z", "T", "IQ"), ]
n <- length(unique(scales$scale))
ggsave("normal_3.pdf", plot_normal(scales), width = 7, height = 7 * (0.30 + 0.028 * n),
       device = cairo_pdf)
```

## PDF

For LaTeX, journals and printing. Use `device = cairo_pdf`: it embeds the font in the file, so the
chart looks the same on every computer and printer, and journals that require embedded fonts accept
it. Without `device`, `ggsave()` uses R's `pdf()` device, which does not embed the font: it names
Helvetica and leaves the program that opens the file to supply it.

```{r pdf, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("normal.pdf", plot_normal(), width = 7, height = 3.2, device = cairo_pdf)
```

In LaTeX, include it at the size it was saved, so that its text keeps its size:

```latex
\includegraphics{normal.pdf}
```

Several charts go into one PDF, one per page, by opening the device yourself and printing each
chart:

```{r pages, eval = FALSE}
cairo_pdf("palettes.pdf", width = 7, height = 3.2, onefile = TRUE)
for (palette in c("blues", "reds", "greens", "diverging")) print(plot_normal(palette = palette))
dev.off()
```

## SVG

For web pages, Markdown files (GitHub shows an SVG in a README like any image) and Word and
PowerPoint in Microsoft 365, which insert SVG files as pictures. There are two ways to write one.

`device = svg`, R's own SVG device, draws every letter as an outline. The chart looks exactly the
same wherever it is opened and no other package is needed, but its text cannot be selected or
edited:

```{r svg, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("normal.svg", plot_normal(), width = 7, height = 3.2, device = svg)
```

The svglite package keeps the text as text, so it can be selected, searched and edited in Inkscape
or Illustrator. It is what `ggsave()` uses for a `.svg` file when `device` is left out, and it has
to be installed first:

```{r svglite, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("svglite")
ggsave("normal.svg", plot_normal(), width = 7, height = 3.2)
```

The program that opens the file draws the text in Arial, so on a computer without Arial another font
takes its place and the labels may shift slightly.

## EMF

For older versions of Word and PowerPoint, which take Windows metafiles but not SVG. The devEMF
package writes them on any system:

```{r emf, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("devEMF")
ggsave("normal.emf", plot_normal(), width = 7, height = 3.2, device = devEMF::emf)
```

## EPS

Some journals still ask for EPS. Use `device = cairo_ps`, which embeds the font:

```{r eps, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("normal.eps", plot_normal(), width = 7, height = 3.2, device = cairo_ps)
```

EPS has no transparency. The chart itself has none, but a layer added with `alpha`, such as the
shaded tails in the [Examples](examples.html) article, is turned into an image inside the file by
`cairo_ps` and left out altogether by `ggsave()`'s default EPS device. Save such charts as PDF or
SVG instead.
